definition: Redress means to set right a wrong or injustice — to correct it and make up for the harm that someone has suffered.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word redress. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know redress should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The tribunal was created to redress the losses of families whose land had been seized without payment.
Acknowledge is weaker than redress: acknowledging a wrong only admits that it happened, while redressing it goes further and actually sets it right.
Undo is stronger than redress: a redressed wrong has been repaired and paid for, but an undone wrong is erased entirely, as though it had never happened at all.

To remedy is to fix a problem or put a bad situation right — you remedy a leak, a shortage, or a mistake, and no one need be at fault. Redress is narrower and heavier: it sets right a wrong done to someone, and it implies making up for the harm suffered.

To recompense is to repay someone for a loss or an effort, often with money and often with no admission that anything unjust occurred. Redress goes further: it treats the loss as a wrong, and it aims to set the whole injustice right rather than merely to write a check.
to fix a wrong so firmly in place that it becomes ever harder to undo
Rather than let the tenants' noise complaints pile up unanswered, the building manager chose to address them at the next meeting, one by one.
Redress means to set right a wrong or injustice — to correct it and make up for the harm that someone has suffered.

When a records check revealed that a scoring error had wrongly failed dozens of nursing students over a decade, the university moved to redress the wrong: it corrected every transcript, refunded the affected semesters, and paid for the licensing exams the graduates had been forced to retake.

The university did more than admit the mistake — it set the injustice right and made up for the harm each student had suffered, and that combination of correcting a wrong and repairing its damage is exactly what redress means.
formal — law, policy, and history writing
Redress takes the wrong itself as its object: you redress an injustice, an imbalance, or the harm done to someone — never the offender, who is punished instead.
A mere technical fault or error is remedied or corrected, not redressed, because no one has been wronged.
The word is common in participle form — a commission charged with redressing historical wrongs — and it doubles as a noun: families who lost their land went to court to seek redress.
